title: Holy, holy, holy
hookLine: Orthodox churches sing Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us

lines: HOLY GOD, HOLY MIGHTY, HOLY IMMORTAL.
cards: Sunday morning in an Orthodox church. Candles, icons, incense hanging in the air, and often no pews, just people standing. At a certain point the choir begins a short chant, and the whole church seems to lean into it.
Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us. Then again. And again.
Three times, sometimes more, slow enough that the words have room. It's short enough to learn on the way home, and its roots go back to a prophet's vision in the Temple.

teach.b: Trisagion: Greek tris, three times, and hagion, holy. The thrice-holy.
In the year King Uzziah died, the prophet Isaiah sees the Lord on a throne, high and lifted up, and creatures called seraphim calling to one another.
In the King James Bible: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Why three times?
Some readers hear Hebrew emphasis: say a word twice and it grows stronger; say it three times and there's nothing left to add. Holy beyond everything.
At the end of the Bible, in Revelation, the song is still going: creatures around the throne "rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come."
The Trisagion turns that cry into three lines people can pray, Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, then one very human request: have mercy on us.
Nobody knows for certain who first put it together. A story people tell, from Constantinople in the fifth century, has an earthquake, and a boy caught up into the sky who heard angels singing it.
What the records do show is bishops crying it out at the Council of Chalcedon, in 451. Orthodox churches sing it at the Divine Liturgy, and Orthodox prayer books open the daily prayers with it.

teach.h: HOLY GOD, HOLY MIGHTY, HOLY IMMORTAL.
teach.b: Catholics sing it too, in Greek and Latin, on Good Friday. Other churches sing Isaiah's three holies in the communion service, the Sanctus, and in a nineteenth-century hymn that begins the same way.
The pattern holds in all of them: first praise beyond words, then a plea for mercy, close to the ground.

how: Orthodox Christians sing the Trisagion in the Divine Liturgy and pray it three times at the start of daily prayers, often making the sign of the cross each time; Catholics sing it on Good Friday, and many churches sing Isaiah's 'Holy, holy, holy' at communion.

games.q: you're Isaiah, in the Temple. you see the Lord high and lifted up, and seraphim calling to each other. what are they saying?
o: holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts.
blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.

games.why: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." the three holies became the root of the Trisagion.

practice: Sit or stand, whichever you like; in Orthodox churches, people often stand to pray. If you pray, say the Trisagion three times, slowly, one line per breath: Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us.
If you don't, say the words as words and notice the shape, something vast, then something small asking for mercy, and after the third time, let the silence hold.
